:::{#thm-many-vectors-dependent}
#### More than $p$ vectors in $\reals^p$ are linearly dependent

If $k > p$, then any $k$ vectors $\vecf{v}_1, \ldots, \vecf{v}_k \in \reals^p$
are not linearly independent (@def-linearly-independent):
some numbers $c_1, \ldots, c_k$, not all zero, satisfy
$c_1 \vecf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_k \vecf{v}_k = \vzero_p$.

:::

::: proof

[Induction](proof-writing.qmd#def-proof-by-induction) on $p$.

**Base case, $p = 1$.**
Each $\vecf{v}_i$ is a single number $v_i$, and $k \ge 2$.
If $v_1 = 0$, take $c_1 = 1$ and every other $c_i = 0$.
Otherwise take $c_1 = v_2$, $c_2 = -v_1$ and every other $c_i = 0$;
then $c_2 \neq 0$, and $v_2 v_1 - v_1 v_2 = 0$.

**Inductive step.**
Let $p \ge 2$,
assume the [theorem](notation.qmd#def-theorem) holds for vectors in $\reals^{p-1}$,
and take $k > p$ vectors in $\reals^p$.
Write $v_{i,p}$ for the last entry of $\vecf{v}_i$.

*Case 1: every $v_{i,p} = 0$.*
Deleting the last entry gives $k > p - 1$ vectors in $\reals^{p-1}$,
which by the inductive hypothesis have a combination
with coefficients not all zero that equals $\vzero_{p-1}$.
The same coefficients combine the original vectors to $\vzero_p$,
since every last entry is $0$.

*Case 2: some $v_{i,p} \neq 0$.*
Renumber the vectors so that $v_{k,p} \neq 0$,
and for $i = 1, \ldots, k-1$ let

$$
\vecf{w}_i \eqdef \vecf{v}_i - \frac{v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,\vecf{v}_k.
$$

The last entry of $\vecf{w}_i$ is
$v_{i,p} - \frac{v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,v_{k,p} = 0$.
Deleting that zero last entry gives $k - 1 > p - 1$ vectors in $\reals^{p-1}$,
so by the inductive hypothesis
there are numbers $c_1, \ldots, c_{k-1}$, not all zero,
whose combination of the shortened vectors is $\vzero_{p-1}$.
Putting the zero last entries back gives
$c_1 \vecf{w}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1} \vecf{w}_{k-1} = \vzero_p$.
Then

$$
\ba
\vzero_p
&= c_1 \vecf{w}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1} \vecf{w}_{k-1}
&& \text{(choice of } c_1, \ldots, c_{k-1} \text{)}
\\
&= \sumto{i}{k-1} c_i \paren{\vecf{v}_i - \frac{v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,\vecf{v}_k}
&& \text{(definition of } \vecf{w}_i \text{)}
\\
&= \sumto{i}{k-1} c_i \vecf{v}_i
 - \sumto{i}{k-1} \frac{c_i v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}\,\vecf{v}_k
&& \text{(distribute each } c_i \text{, and split the sum)}
\\
&= c_1 \vecf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_{k-1} \vecf{v}_{k-1}
 - \paren{\sumto{i}{k-1} \frac{c_i v_{i,p}}{v_{k,p}}}\,\vecf{v}_k,
&& \text{(factor } \vecf{v}_k \text{ out of the second sum)}
\ea
$$

a combination of $\vecf{v}_1, \ldots, \vecf{v}_k$ equal to $\vzero_p$
whose first $k - 1$ coefficients are not all zero.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-many-vectors-dependent}
#### Three vectors in $\reals^2$

@thm-many-vectors-dependent says the three vectors
$(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 1)$ in $\reals^2$ are linearly dependent,
and indeed $1 \cd (1, 0) + 1 \cd (0, 1) - 1 \cd (1, 1) = (0, 0)$.
The theorem says nothing about $k \le p$ vectors:
$(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ are linearly independent,
while $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 4)$ are not (@exm-linearly-independent).

:::
